schema.missing-pk: Table {table} has no primary key declared.
schema.fk-no-index: The foreign key ({columns}) of table {table} has no index starting with these columns, so deleting or updating a row in the parent table may have to scan all of {table}.
schema.float-money: Column {column} of table {table} uses type {type}. Floating-point types can make money amounts drift when rounded.
schema.varchar-too-large: Column {column} of table {table} declares length {length}, above {threshold}. MySQL reserves the full declared length for temporary tables and sorting; PostgreSQL pays no extra, but a large length often means no real limit was chosen.

evidence.scanSeq: In the scenario that ran, table {table} was read with a full table scan ({scan}). This is what was observed; it does not prove the rule is the cause, since the planner may also scan a small table fully.
evidence.scanIndex: In the scenario that ran, table {table} was read with an index ({scan}). The result only holds for the statement and data that ran.
evidence.estimatedScanSeq: The statement did not run. By the optimizer estimate, table {table} will be read with a full table scan ({scan}).
evidence.estimatedScanIndex: The statement did not run. By the optimizer estimate, table {table} will be read with an index ({scan}).
evidence.counts: This node read {rows} rows and {pages} pages.
evidence.estimatedRows: The optimizer estimates this node returns about {rows} rows.
evidence.structureOnly: Described from the structure in your SQL. No scenario has run to show that this structure breaks.
evidence.indexUnrelated: In the scenario that ran, table {table} was read with an index ({scan}), but that step does not filter on column {column}. What was observed is a different index serving the statement, so this run neither confirms nor rules out the rule.
